generic_skills: Predicting outcomes and making reasoned decisions
Working with others to generate ideas
Looking for patterns and making generalisation
Talking confidently and explaining ideas/opinions clearly
Using a range of media to communicate ideas
Using mathematics to justify and support decisions
Using technology to create, manipulate and process information
Using technology to collaborate, communicate and refine work
Respectfully responding to people of all cultures
Appreciating ethnicity as a cradle for creativity and innovation
values: Honesty, upholding and defending the truth at all times
Justice and fairness in dealing with others
Integrity; moral uprightness and sound character

themes.theme_description: Competency: The learner analyses stoichiometric relationships, evaluates experimental methods, and synthesises solutions to complex chemical problems.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Masses of Atoms and Molecules, Accurate Relative Atomic Masses

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: evaluate the relationship between atomic masses and isotopic abundances in calculating accurate relative atomic masses. (u, s)
synthesise methods to determine accurate relative atomic mass using given isotopic data. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners discuss atomic masses, isotopes, and relative atomic masses. Use real examples from the Periodic Table.

As a whole class, learners watch a video on the working of a mass spectrometer or individually, search for information about the working of the spectrometer and its application in daily life, discuss their findings in groups, and make presentations.
In groups, learners carry out activities to interpret isotopic data such as isotope masses and relative abundance and use it to calculate relative atomic masses.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners' group discussion session to assess their levels of interaction, confidence, and respect for one another’s opinions.
Ask learners to find their level of understanding of the relationship between the atomic masses and isotopic masses of an element.
Review learners' written responses to assess their coherence in explaining how to obtain relative atomic mass from isotopic masses.
Observe learners’ level of attention and participation in group discussions and presentations.
Engage the learners in discussions to assess their comprehension of the working of the mass spectrometer and interpretation of data.
Evaluate learners' written calculations for accuracy when determining relative atomic masses from isotopic masses.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the concept of the mole as a fundamental unit of measurement for chemical substances and perform complex mole calculations in chemical reactions. (u, s)
formulate strategies for calculating moles in compounds and reactions. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners use prior knowledge to discuss Avogadro’s number and the mole concept using visuals to illustrate these ideas.
In pairs, learners will complete worksheets with tasks involving the calculation of moles in chemical reactions.
In pairs, learners use a problem-based approach to solve multi-step mole calculation exercises in different contexts (emphasise correct units).

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Check learners’ confidence and collaboration in the group discussion.
Engage learners in a discussion to assess their reasoning about strategies used in calculations.
Assess the accuracy of calculations.
Check learners’ participation activities involving solving problems on the mole concept.
Probe learners to assess their reasoning regarding the methodology in solving problems on mole concepts.
Evaluate learners’ accuracy and the coherence of written responses.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: construct balanced chemical equations for given reactions, including synthesis, decomposition, and combustion reactions. (u, s)
critically examine the relationships between empirical and molecular formulae in representing compounds. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners use prior knowledge to practice and demonstrate balancing equations with correct formulae and state symbols.
In groups, learners perform experiments to determine the empirical formula of magnesium oxide.
In groups, learners use worksheets to determine empirical and molecular formulae through a series of problem sets and contextual applications.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor learners’ level of involvement in completing tasks on writing balanced equations.
Question learners to evaluate their reasoning in writing balanced equations.
Review the accuracy of the balanced equations and the correctness of formulae.
Evaluate learners’ ability to organise, plan and manipulate apparatus during laboratory activities.
Probe learners’ reasoning to assess the level of understanding of the relationship between empirical and molecular formulae.
Assess learners’ solutions to problems on formulae for accuracy.

practicals.title: Determination of empirical formula of magnesium oxide
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners perform experiments to determine the empirical formula of magnesium oxide.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Solutions and Concentration, Calculations Involving Gas Volumes

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the principles of concentration and gas laws to accurately calculate molarity and gas volumes in various solutions and reactions. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information on the preparation of standard solutions and their use in calculations, discuss their findings in their groups, and make reports.
In groups, learners carry out experiments to prepare solutions of different molarities and use them to standardise other solutions.
In groups, learners use worksheets to carry out calculations involving Gay-Lussac’s and Avogadro’s laws to determine amounts of substances.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor learners as they make presentations, checking the accuracy of their submissions.
Ask learners to explain gas law principles and molarity to assess their understanding of the concept.
Evaluate learners' written solutions to calculations for consistency and accuracy.

practicals.title: Preparation and standardisation of solutions
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out experiments to prepare solutions of different molarities and use them to standardise other solutions.

themes.theme_description: Competency: The learner deduces electronic configurations, evaluates their implications for chemical properties and bonding, and synthesises models to predict atomic behaviour in various contexts.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Electron Configurations of Atoms and Ions

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rule to write electronic configurations of atoms and ions and use them to predict reactivity. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners use the Internet, demonstration videos, or suitable textbooks to search for information on principles of writing electronic configurations, discuss their findings in groups, and write electronic configurations of atoms and ions.
In groups, learners use visual aids such as energy level diagrams to illustrate principles of writing electronic configurations.
In pairs, learners use a problem-based approach to carry out exercises involving writing configurations of selected atoms and ions and predicting reactivity.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Watch learners as they discuss to assess their confidence and respect for one another’s opinion while determining electronic configurations.
Engage learners in a discussion to assess their level of conceptualisation of the s, p, d and f principles of writing electronic configurations.
Evaluate the written electronic configurations for the correct application of s, p, d and f principles.

suggested_uses: Individually, learners use the Internet, demonstration videos... to search for information

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: examine the nature and types of radioactive decay and apply this knowledge to predict decay rates and half-lives in specific elements. (k, u, s)

evaluate the principles of radioactivity in real-life applications, such as in medicine, industry, and environmental science and the associated health, environmental, and ethical implications of radioactive materials. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search for information about radioactive decay, nuclear stability, decay rates, and half-life, discuss their findings, and carry out related calculations.
In groups, learners use a problem-based approach to solve mathematical problems on radioactive decay and half-life.
Individually, learners search for information about applications and effects of radioactivity, discuss their findings in groups and make presentations.
In groups, learners analyse case studies on applications of radioactivity in real life.
Learners engage in a class debate to evaluate the ethical and related safety implications of radioactivity.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Evaluate the level of participation in group discussions.
Engage learners in discussions to assess how much they know about applications and effects.
Assess the accuracy and coherence of written responses to problems on radioactive decay and half-life.
Monitor the level of involvement of learners in the group discussions and debate.
Ask learners to explain the safety and ethical implications of radioactivity to assess their appreciation.
Evaluate the reports of the learners and debate for the accuracy of facts and coherence.

themes.theme_description: Competency: The learner analyses the types of chemical bonds and molecular structures, and relates them to the properties and uses of substances in real-life contexts.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Formation of Ionic and Metallic Bonds

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: justify the formation of ionic and metallic bonds based on electron transfer and electrostatic forces. (u, s)
evaluate the properties of ionic and metallic compounds in relation to bond strength and structural composition. (u)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners use prior knowledge to design models illustrating electron transfer in ionic bonding and electron pooling in metallic bonding.

Individually, learners search for information about the properties of ionic and metallic bonds, their relative strengths, and how they relate to their properties, discuss in their groups, and make presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Check the level of planning, manipulation, creativity, accuracy, and participation in hands-on model building.
Discuss with the learners to assess understanding of the relationship between properties, structure, and bond strength.
Evaluate the accuracy, creativity, and clarity of the models.
Monitor the learners’ involvement and respect for one another’s opinions in the discussion groups.
Check the learners’ understanding of the relationship between properties of substances and bond strength by asking probing questions.
Assess the learners’ written reports for accuracy and coherence.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the formation of covalent bonds including dative covalency and explain molecular structures by applying VSEPR theory to predict molecular shapes and bond angles. (u, s)
analyse the polarity of molecules based on molecular structure and electron distribution. (u)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about covalent bonding, dative covalency, and the principles of VSEPR theory, discuss their findings in groups, and make presentations.
In groups, learners predict, draw shapes of molecules and ions, and build 3D molecular models based on VSEPR theory.

Individually, learners search for information about the bond and molecular polarity in relation to differences in electronegativity with emphasis on hydrogen bonding and Van der Waal’s forces, discuss their findings in their groups, and make reports.
In pairs, learners use problem-based methods to carry out exercises involving different molecular structures and their properties and make reports.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ discussion about covalent bonding to assess the level of interaction and how confidently they present their ideas.
Probe the learners to justify how they applied VSEPR theory to draw and design molecular shapes and models.
Evaluate learners’ drawn models and structures for accuracy.
Monitor the learners as they discuss molecular and bond polarity to assess their level of confidence and clarity of facts.
Probe the learners to assess their understanding of the difference between bond and molecular polarity.
Evaluate the reports for accuracy and coherence.

themes.theme_description: Topic competency: The learner analyses the trends and periodic properties of elements, to explain and predict the reactivity and properties of elements in the Periodic Table.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: evaluate how the Periodic Table is organised based on atomic number and properties, recognising its historical significance. (u, s)
analyse the position of elements to predict their chemical behaviour, considering periodic trends. (u, s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners watch a video or search for information on the historical development of the Periodic Table (from Mendeleev’s design to Mosely’s atomic concept), discuss its organisation, and write group reports.

In groups, learners use samples of the modern Periodic Table to explore, discuss its organisation and respond to specific tasks such as identifying similarities in blocks, groups and periods (use the IUPAC form with 18 groups).
In groups, the learners use an inquiry-based approach to predict trends in properties such as reactivity based on element positions and make reports.
Learners engage in problem-solving tasks where they predict the reactivity of unknown elements based on the position of elements in the Periodic Table.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners’ level of engagement in group discussions.
Ask the learners to articulate the historical reasons for certain arrangements in the Periodic Table to clear any misconceptions.
Evaluate written reports of the learners for coherence and accuracy.
Observe the learners to assess their reasoning skills and teamwork during discussions.
Engage the learners in one-on-one discussions to gauge their understanding of trends.
Collect and review the learners’ predictions on element behaviour for accuracy.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Variation in Trends of Properties Across Periods and the Diagonal Relationships

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the periodic physical and chemical properties in the Periodic Table, identifying patterns and exceptions. (u, s)
justify the variation in physical and chemical properties across period 3, incorporating diagonal relationships. (u, s v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the periodic physical properties of elements in the Periodic Table (melting point, atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, electropositivity), discuss their findings in groups and make joint reports.
Learners apply the jigsaw method by working in groups, with each group focusing on one trend and teaching it to the rest of the class.

In groups, learners use data sets of periodic trends (ionisation energy, electron affinity, atomic radius, ionic radius, electronegativity) to analyse and graph this data to infer relationships and patterns, identifying exceptions.

Learners individually search for information about the physical properties of period 3 elements (physical state, melting points, structure and bonding, metallic character), discuss their findings in groups and present reports.
Learners apply problem-based learning to analyse sets of data relating to the physical properties of elements in period 3.

In groups, learners conduct laboratory activities where they observe chemical properties (reactivity with water, dilute acids and alkali) of elements like sodium, magnesium, and aluminium and sulphur. Record observations, draw inferences and present their reports.

Individually, learners search for information about the oxides (structure and bonding, melting points, reaction with dilute acids, alkalis and water) and chlorides (structure and bonding, melting points, reaction with dilute acids, alkalis and water) of period 3 elements, discuss their findings in groups and present reports.
In groups, learners carry out test tube experiments to identify magnesium and aluminium ions.
Individually, learners search for information about diagonal relationships between lithium and magnesium and also between beryllium and aluminium.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor participation in group discussions.
Ask probing questions to evaluate understanding of trends and exceptions.
Evaluate data interpretations and completed plotted graphs for comprehension of trends.
Observe the learners to assess the level of participation in group discussions and data analysis.
Ask questions to assess understanding of physical and chemical properties of period 3 elements and their compounds.
Assess group presentations and reports for accuracy and depth of understanding.

practicals.title: Chemical properties of period 3 elements
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners conduct laboratory activities where they observe chemical properties (reactivity with water, dilute acids and alkali) of elements like sodium, magnesium, and aluminium and sulphur.

practicals.title: Identification of magnesium and aluminium ions
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out test tube experiments to identify magnesium and aluminium ions.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Trends in Properties of Group 2 Elements

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: investigate the reactivity and properties of Group 2 elements and their compounds in relation to their applications in industry. (s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the physical properties (melting point, metallic radii and density) of Group 2 elements, discuss their findings in groups and make reports.
In pairs, learners use problem-based learning to interpret data on the physical properties of Group 2 elements.
In groups, learners carry out experiments to investigate the reactivity of Group 2 metals with air, water and dilute acids.
In groups, learners carry out laboratory experiments to investigate solubility, effect of heat and action of dilute acids on compounds of Group 2 (hydroxides, sulphates, nitrates and carbonates).
In pairs, learners carry out test tube experiments to identify ions in Group 2 compounds.
Individually, learners search for information on the applications of Group 2 elements and their compounds, discuss their findings in groups and make presentations.
In groups, learners carry out projects to make different industrial products from Group 2 compounds.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Assess learners' skills in planning, manipulation of apparatus and safety management during experiments.
Probe learners’ opinions, methodology used in experiments and assess knowledge of linkages of the metals to industrial uses.
Evaluate group presentations and reports for the accuracy, depth and coherence.

practicals.title: Reactivity of Group 2 metals
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out experiments to investigate the reactivity of Group 2 metals with air, water and dilute acids.

practicals.title: Properties of Group 2 compounds
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out laboratory experiments to investigate solubility, effect of heat and action of dilute acids on compounds of Group 2 (hydroxides, sulphates, nitrates and carbonates).

practicals.title: Identification of Group 2 ions
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners carry out test tube experiments to identify ions in Group 2 compounds.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out projects to make different industrial products from Group 2 compounds.

themes.theme_description: Topic competency: The learner analyses and evaluates thermodynamic principles and processes to predict the spontaneity and feasibility of chemical reactions and processes.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: synthesise energy profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, explaining the concept of enthalpy change. (u, s)
evaluates the role of activation energy in reaction mechanisms using energy profile diagrams. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners use prior knowledge to discuss, draw and explain energy profiles for endothermic and exothermic reactions.
In pairs, learners carry out experiments to demonstrate exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Individually, learners search for information about activation energy, discuss their findings in groups and make reports.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor and assess the learners’ planning, manipulation and safety management skills during experiments.
Ask the learners to explain the differences between exothermic and endothermic reactions to check their knowledge of the concepts.
Assess drawn energy profiles for correct depiction and explanations.
Monitor the learners’ level of participation in group discussions.
Assess the learners’ understanding of activation energy by asking them key questions.
Evaluate drawn diagrams for accurate representation of activation energy changes, reports for accuracy and coherence.

practicals.title: Demonstration of exothermic and endothermic reactions
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners carry out experiments to demonstrate exothermic and endothermic reactions.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Types of Enthalpy Changes and Hess’s Law

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse different types of enthalpy changes and the conditions under which they occur, including their significance in thermochemical equations. (k, u)
apply Hess’s law to calculate unknown enthalpy changes using energy cycles and enthalpy data. (s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about enthalpy of reaction, formation, atomisation, bond energy, combustion, and neutralisation, with real-life examples, and discuss, in groups, their findings.
Learners explore Hess's law by drawing simple energy cycle diagrams to deduce expected energy changes.
In pairs, learners are engaged in problem-solving exercises using thermochemical equations.
In pairs, learners engage in exercises where they apply Hess’s law by using energy cycle diagrams, and thermochemical equations to solve given tasks.
Individually, learners practise constructing energy cycle diagrams to apply Hess's law.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor the learners to assess the level of interaction and how they confidently express themselves in group discussions.
Probe the learners to assess their understanding of the different types of enthalpies of reaction.
Assess the accuracy of learners’ responses to the problem-solving exercises.
Observe the learners to assess their level of engagement and participation in solving problems.
Assess the learners’ ability to justify the use of energy cycle diagrams and thermochemical equations by asking key questions.
Assess the learners’ responses to the tasks for accuracy.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the concept of lattice energy, its role in the formation of ionic compounds, and describe the steps involved in constructing Born-Haber cycles. (k, u, s)
apply Born-Haber cycles to solve problems involving the calculation of lattice energies and related thermodynamic quantities. (s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information on the concept of lattice energy, factors affecting lattice energy, its role in the formation of ionic compounds, and how it can be calculated using the Born-Haber cycle, discuss their findings in groups, and make a report.
In pairs, learners engage in practice exercises involving the calculation of lattice enthalpies.
In pairs, learners engage in problem-solving exercises involving the relationship between lattice energy, hydration energy, and enthalpy of solution.
In groups, learners use case studies to analyse sets of data on lattice energy to predict the stability of ionic compounds.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor the learners to assess the levels of participation in group discussions about Born-Haber cycles involving lattice energies.
Ask the learners to explain the concept of lattice energy and the steps in Born-Haber cycles to assess their understanding.
Evaluate the learners’ reports for skill of drawing Born-Haber cycles and the correctness of responses to practice exercises.
Check the learners’ level of engagement in finding solutions to tasks in exercises.
Ask the learners to explain the methodology used in solving problems in the exercises.
Evaluate the learners’ written responses to tasks for accuracy.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply principles of organic chemistry to understand the classification and general characteristics of organic compounds, including functional groups, homologous series, and the concept of isomerism. (k, u)
use IUPAC nomenclature to name different organic compounds. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the unique nature of carbon in organic compounds, such as how single, double, and triple bonds are formed, and engage in a teacher-led discussion.
In groups, learners use molecular models to demonstrate functional groups and homologous series.
In groups, learners use models to illustrate different types of isomers and create models of isomers for a given molecular formula and display their work.
In groups, learners engage in a teacher-guided discussion to explain the different properties of isomers.
In pairs, learners practise naming and drawing organic molecules following IUPAC rules.
In groups, learners analyse molecular structures to identify functional groups.
Individually, learners carry out problem-solving exercises involving structure prediction based on functional groups.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor the learners’ confidence, accuracy of facts, and involvement during the teacher-led discussion about the unique nature of carbon.
Discuss with the learners to assess justification for the choice of materials used in making the models.
Assess the accuracy of responses to practice exercises involving drawing and naming simple organic compounds.
Observe the process of drawing and naming organic compounds to assess learners’ interaction and participation.
Question the learners to assess their knowledge of using IUPAC in naming organic compounds.
Assess the correctness of responses to written exercises requiring the use of IUPAC nomenclature.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply principles of organic chemistry to differentiate between alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes, and explain their physical properties based on molecular structure. (k, u)
predict the reactivity and reaction mechanisms of alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes. (s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the physical properties of alkanes, alkenes, and alkynes, discuss their findings in groups, and make reports.
In groups, learners use molecular models to demonstrate bonding and structure in hydrocarbons.
In groups, learners carry out laboratory experiments to observe the physical properties of the various functional groups of hydrocarbons (e.g. solubility, melting point).

Individually, learners search for information about the reactivity and reaction mechanisms of alkanes (UV-catalysed chlorination), alkenes (hydrogen, hydrogen halides, acidified water, halogens), polymerisation and oxidation using potassium manganate (VII), discuss their findings in their groups and make reports.
In pairs, learners carry out test tube reactions to identify the double bond in alkenes using bromine water and potassium manganate (VII).
In pairs, learners practise the writing of reactions and their mechanisms using worksheets.
In groups, learners use case studies to explore the different applications of alkenes and alkynes in everyday life and make reports.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners during laboratory experiments to assess the planning, manipulation of apparatus and safety management skills.
Probe the learners to assess their skills in interpreting results from experiments on functional groups of hydrocarbons.
Assess the learners’ reports from experiments and discussions for accuracy and coherence.
Observe the learners’ discussions on reactivity and mechanisms of hydrocarbons to assess interaction and confidence in presentation.
Discuss with the learners to assess their understanding of the principle of writing addition reaction mechanisms.
Evaluate written reports and mechanisms of reactions of hydrocarbons for accuracy and coherence.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: (NB: Addition reactions of alkenes are similar to those of alkynes).

practicals.title: Physical properties of hydrocarbons
practicals.description_verbatim: In groups, learners carry out laboratory experiments to observe the physical properties of the various functional groups of hydrocarbons (e.g. solubility, melting point).

practicals.title: Identification of double bond in alkenes
practicals.description_verbatim: In pairs, learners carry out test tube reactions to identify the double bond in alkenes using bromine water and potassium manganate (VII).

themes.theme_description: Competency: The learner analyses the structures, functional groups, and reactivity of organic compounds, and applies knowledge of organic reactions and organic reaction mechanisms to synthesise organic molecules.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the structure and properties of alkyl halides in terms of their reactivity with different reagents, identifying substitution and elimination reactions. (k, u, s)
evaluate the uses and impacts of alkyl halides in industrial processes. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the structure, nomenclature, and physical properties of alkyl halides, discuss their findings in groups, and make reports.

Individually, learners search for information about the chemical properties of alkyl halides with different reagents (alkali, cyanide, ammonia, alcoholic alkali, reaction with metals), including synthesis, discuss their findings in their groups and make reports.
In groups, learners create a visual map comparing substitution and elimination mechanisms, including key factors (e.g. reagents, solvents, temperature).
In groups, learners analyse case studies involving the role of alkyl halides in industry, including environmental impacts, and discuss and make presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor discussions of the learners about alkyl halides to assess learners’ involvement and the ability to develop visual maps.
Discuss with the learners to assess their understanding of the industrial impact and ethical considerations regarding products from alkyl halides.
Assess the learners’ reports on the physical and chemical properties of alkyl halides for accuracy of facts and coherence.
Monitor discussions and presentations to assess participation, accuracy of facts, and respect for others.
Discuss with the learners to assess their understanding of the role of the alkyl halides in industry.
Evaluate the learners' reports for accuracy of facts about the role of alkyl halides and their impact on the environment.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: compare benzene and methyl benzene in terms of structure, stability, and reactivity in electrophilic substitution reactions. (k, u, s)
analyse the environmental and health impacts of benzene derivatives. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about the structures of benzene, and methylbenzene in terms of their stability and reactivity. They discuss their findings in groups and make reports.
In groups, learners discuss the difference between electrophilic substitution reactions involving benzene and methyl benzene, and make a report.
In pairs, learners practice writing equations and mechanisms of electrophilic substitution reactions involving benzene and methylbenzene.
In groups, learners analyse case studies involving the effects of benzene derivatives on health and the environment and discuss and present written reports.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor the learners’ discussion to assess engagement and communication skills during discussions to understand the structures of benzene and methyl benzene.
Engage the learners in discussions to assess their understanding of the difference between benzene and methyl benzene in terms of structure, stability and reactivity.
Evaluate the accuracy of learners’ reports, written equations, and mechanisms of reactions.
Assess the learners’ participation in a discussion involving analysing the health and environmental impact of benzene derivatives.
Ask the learners to assess their knowledge of the impact of benzene derivatives on health and the environment.
Assess the accuracy of the learners’ reports about the effects of benzene derivatives on health and the environment.

themes.theme_description: Competency: The learner analyses principles of chemical equilibrium and applies them to explain and solve problems related to industrial processes, ionic equilibria, buffer systems, and solubility equilibria in various chemical and real-world contexts.

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: (derivation of the relationship between Kc and Kp not required)

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: evaluate the dynamic nature of chemical equilibrium and determination of equilibrium constants. (k, u, s)
predict how closed systems respond to stress, by applying Le Chatelier's principle. (u, s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners’ search for information about conditions for equilibrium, characteristics of the dynamic equilibrium, nature of chemical equilibrium systems, types of chemical equilibrium and equilibrium constants, discuss their findings in groups, and make presentations.
Learners carry out experiments to determine Kc involving the esterification of ethanol and ethanoic acid using concentrated sulphuric acid.
In groups, learners use worksheets to discuss and solve mathematical problems about Kc and Kp.
Individually, learners search for information about the different factors that affect chemical equilibria, discuss their findings in groups and make presentations.
In groups, learners use digital simulation tools such as PhET to explore equilibrium dynamics by modifying conditions and observing shifts.
In pairs, learners use worksheets to practice solving problems involving Le Chatelier’s principle and predict shifts.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners to assess their planning, manipulation of apparatus, safety management skills and respect for one another during laboratory work.
Discuss with the learners to assess their interpretation of observations from laboratory work.
Evaluate written responses of the learners for accuracy of calculations of Kc and Kp.
Check the learners’ skills of ICT proficiency in using digital software to explore equilibrium dynamics.
Probe the learners to assess their methodology in completing worksheet tasks involving Le Chatelier’s principle.
Assess the correctness of the learners’ reports on practising problems involving Le Chatelier’s principle.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: (derivation of the relationship between Kc and Kp not required)

practicals.title: Determination of Kc
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners carry out experiments to determine Kc involving the esterification of ethanol and ethanoic acid using concentrated sulphuric acid.

suggested_uses: In groups, learners use digital simulation tools such as PhET to explore equilibrium dynamics by modifying conditions and observing shifts.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: evaluate how temperature, concentration, and pressure influence chemical equilibrium and propose methods to optimise reaction conditions in industrial applications. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners discuss real-life applications of equilibrium shifts, such as in industrial processes.
In groups, learners analyse industrial applications of chemical equilibria, such as the Haber process and contact process where equilibrium control is essential.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Monitor the learners to assess their confidence in expression and interaction during discussions about real-life applications of chemical equilibria.
Discuss with the learners to assess their understanding of the application of chemical equilibria in industry.
Assess the learners’ reports about the application of chemical equilibria for accuracy and coherence.

topic_metadata.topic_title: Ionic Equilibrium, Hydrolysis of Salts and Buffer Solutions

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the concepts of ionic equilibrium, including the dissociation of acids and bases, the pH scale, the hydrolysis of salts, and how buffer solutions maintain pH stability in chemical systems. (k, u, s)
evaluate the role of buffer solutions in biological and environmental systems, predicting their behaviour under acidic or basic conditions. (u, a/v)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Individually, learners search for information about theories of acids and bases, acid and base dissociation constants, and pH calculation, discuss their findings, and make reports.
In pairs, learners apply problem-based learning to perform practice exercises to solve mathematical problems involving pH and dissociation constants.
Individually, learners search for information about the hydrolysis of salts and hydrolysis constants, discuss their findings, and make reports.
In pairs, learners apply problem-based learning to carry out practice exercises to solve mathematical problems involving hydrolysis constants.
Individually, learners search for information about buffer solutions, their preparation, mode of action, and pH calculation, discuss their findings and make reports.
In groups, learners perform laboratory experiments to prepare buffer solutions of a given (pH).
In pairs, learners use worksheets to practise solving mathematical problems involving the (pH) of buffer solutions.
Individually, learners search for information on the role of buffer solutions in biological and environmental systems, discuss their findings in groups, and make presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the learners as they carry out laboratory experiments to assess their level of interaction within the group.
Discuss with the learners to assess their understanding of theories of acids and bases.
Assess written reports of the learners from discussion and practice exercises for accuracy and coherence.
